title: Key takeaways from Solar & Storage Live UK, Birmingham - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
At Solar & Storage Live UK, industry leaders highlighted financing, skills shortages and community engagement as key challenges for the country’s growing pipeline of large-scale solar projects. The event also showcased opportunities in plug-in solar and residential battery storage, supported by policy measures and rising household energy costs.
Matthew Lynas
28 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Residential
Utility-scale
(From left) pv magazine Editor Matthew Lynas; Simon Wheeler, Development Director, Enso Energy; Tracey Elliot, Director Eden Sustainable Power; Ben Fawcett, Head of Business Development UK, Lightsource BP; David Hoare, Technical Director, RSK.
UK developers have gotten very good at securing planning consent for 100 MW+ solar projects, but who is going to build them?
That was the question at the heart of a
pv magazine
moderated panel held at Solar & Storage Live UK in Birmingham. The September trade is the largest exhibition and conference for the industry in the country.
It was a lively session at the keynote Keynote Stage for the “Delivering the NSIP pipeline” panel discussion, which focused on the practicalities of building out Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) solar – projects of 100 MW or greater – as well as utility-scale solar projects more generally.
Like in many mature solar markets, securing planning consent is not the toughest challenge facing a UK solar project. Reaching financial close remains the major hurdle for utility-scale solar, but when asked if there is a disconnect between government ambition on clean energy and the revenue support on offer, Ben Fawcett, head of business development UK at Lightsource bp, warned that policymakers must do more to give investors revenue visibility for large-scale projects.
Despite a recent run of successful contracts for difference (CfD) auctions for solar, in which
new records
were set for procured capacity, Fawcett said the industry needs to see a ninth CfD tender if it is to secure the contracted revenues that will allow investors to back a growing pipeline of large-scale projects.
Skill shortage was another focus of the session. Large-scale assets require lots of skilled labor, and as more solar projects are connected to the transmission network the talent pool for engineers permitted to work at extra-high voltages could come under pressure.
Tracey Elliot, director at Eden Sustainable, recalled how previous periods of high-volume solar construction in the United Kingdom had relied on overseas labor. Creating skilled, meaningful work in the United Kingdom should be a focus according to Elliot and could go some way to building community support for developments.
David Hoare, technical director at RSK Group took the question of community objection further. RSK Group has worked on 40 NSIP projects that have secured development consent orders (DCOs), so the company has experience on delivering planning consent. Hoare warned that the industry standard approached to consultation until now – a kind of church hall diplomacy – may not be enough in the future, calling for developers to more actively engage with locals to overcome objections to large-scale solar.
A packed Wednesday morning session at Solar & Storage Live UK delved into the challenges facing utility-scale solar developers.
Despite the value of better consultation practices and the potential for developers to create new jobs roles, Simon Wheeler, director of development at Enso Energy, closed the session by warning that what the industry needs is regulatory stability, with no new mandatory provisions for solar developers who already have enough to manage when building major infrastructure projects.
Utility-scale was not the only focus at Solar & Storage Live UK, and the 2026 event followed the August introduction of
plug-in solar regulations
allowing consumers to self-install arrays up to 800 W. Despite the quick regulation change for plug-in solar modules – the UK government first committed to plug-in solar in February 2026 – there was a sense from some stands that this is an policy that has only been half cooked.
A plug-in solar solution from AP Systems on display in Birmingham. UK regulations do not yet allow consumers to install plug-in battery storage. | Image: pv magazine
In leading plug-in markets such as Germany, consumers can buy and install plug-in solar and plug-in battery storage, however the UK regulations have not been updated to allow amateurs to install energy storage in this format. That’s a limiting factor in a market where energy storage attachment rates are growing. Solutions on the stands at Solar & Storage Live UK amounted to modules with a microinverter that connects to the households using a British Standards three-in plug, although there were plug-in battery products that could be seen. The manufacturers are ready, but an ongoing consultation on plug-in battery safety means it could be more than a year before regulations are implemented.
Despite this, one manufacturer told
pv magazine
they had good conversations with retailers and wholesalers on the exhibition floor. Plug-in devices have yet to make a splash on the UK high street – but major retailers have
previously shown enthusiasm
for the products, and more may appear on shelf soon.
The residential segment is also on track to benefit from a ramping up of policy support, with grants available through the UK government’s Warm Home Grants program, and more attractive financing terms expected soon through the Warm Home Loans – a government program that will see the state subsidize the risk of a solar loan, lowering the interest rate paid by consumers on their financed installation.
UK consumers also face a 4% energy price hike from 1 October when the price cap enforced by regulator Ofgem comes into force. The energy price cap protects around 22 million UK households on default tariffs by limiting the maximum rates and standing charges that energy suppliers can charge. Under the current price cap a typical households pays GBP 1,663 ($2,200) per year on gas and electricity, meaning the 4% increase would take an average bill to GBP 1,723 per year. There was an expectation among some exhibitors at Solar & Storage Live that even higher energy bills combined with anxiety over conflict in the Middle East will result in more retrofit solar and energy storage installations.
On energy storage, the United Kingdom has been a pioneering market for utility-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) for some time and despite a challenging grid connections process, the pipeline remains significantly oversupplied. New measures such as introducing
financial commitments for pipeline projects
are expected in a bid to further rationalize the connections queue.
Residential energy storage has entered a major growth phase, and battery storage is now often installed without solar. Australian solar consultancy SunWiz showed
pv magazine
data at the show revealing standalone energy storage installations now exceed standalone solar in the United Kingdom. While the data did not distinguish between retrofits to buildings with existing PV systems or installations on buildings without solar, the opportunity to arbitrage energy via time-of-use tariffs offered by major UK utilities is making the case for household battery storage stronger.
Solar and Storage Live UK was held across Sept. 22-24 at the Birmingham National Exhibition Centre (NEC) The show will return to the Birmingham NEC on Sept. 21-23, 2027.

title: Global solar additions hit 690 GW in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Latest report from IEA-PVPS says the world’s cumulative solar capacity reached 2.96 TWh by the end of last year, a total theoretically capable of generating around 12% of global electricity consumption.
Patrick Jowett
28 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Global solar additions reached around 690 GW in 2025, according to the latest report from the International Energy Agency’s Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme (IEA-PVPS).
IEA-PVPS’
Trends in Photovoltaic Applications 2026
report reveals last year’s additions represented a 15% increase on installations during 2024.
China installed 415 GW, or 60%, of global installations last year. India ranked second for annual additions, at 54 GW, followed by the United States (43 GW), Germany (18 GW) and Pakistan (14 GW). Collectively, the European Union added 68 GW.
The report notes that PV deployment continued to broaden geographically, with 36 countries installing more than 1 GW of solar, three more than in 2024.
Centralised solar systems accounted for 410 GW of new solar systems last year, led by China (256 GW), India (42 GW), USA (35 GW), Spain (11 GW) and Germany (8.3 GW). The report also notes Saudi Arabia and the UAE’s as growing markets that are driven by centralised systems.
Distributed solar accounted for 282 GW of new installations in 2025, a record for the market segment, up from 228 GW in 2024.
China deployed 159 GW of all distributed solar last year, followed by Pakistan (14 GW), India (12 GW), Germany (9.2 GW) and Brazil (7.9 GW). The report lists France, Türkiye, Japan and Australia as other countries where the distributed market is driving overall growth.
Last year saw Australia surpass the Netherlands as the country with the highest cumulative installed PV capacity per inhabitant, with 1,604 W/cap compared to 1,584 W/cap. Germany ranks third in this metric, with 1,413 W/cap.
An additional eight European countries – Spain, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Lithuania, Estonia, Switzerland and Belgium – are above 1,000 W/cap. China’s penetration rate also moved beyond this threshold, to stand at 1,040 W/cap.
In the report’s forward, co-managers of IEA-PVPS Task 1, Melodie de l’Epine and Izumi Kaizuka, and IEA-PVPS chair, Daniel Mugnier, wrote that last year’s deployments “continued alongside significant industrial imbalance.”
They explain that module production remains above annual installations figure, while low utilisation rates, continuing price pressure and weak profitability impact manufacturers throughout the value chain.
Figures from the report state that global production of solar modules reached 722 GW last year, a 0.6% decrease on 2024. This represents a slowdown on the 61.7% year-on-year growth recorded between 2022 and 2023.
China accounted for 79% of global PV module production last year. The country’s global share dropped from 86% in 2024 as manufacturing capacity expanded in India and the USA.
Global PV module manufacturing capacity is estimated to have reached 1,531 GW/year last year, of which 71% was located in China.
de l’Epine, Kaizuka and Mugnier added that the scale of solar deployment is changing the relationship between solar capacity, electricity systems and electricity markets.
“Curtailment, negative prices, declining capture prices and grid connection constraints are more increasingly visible in high penetration markets,” they said. “Storage, flexible demand, stronger networks, improved forecasting and appropriate market access are becoming essential to extending the contribution of PV beyond the hours in which it generates.”
Additional figures from the report highlight the considerable growth in storage deployment. Annual battery energy storage capacity additions across Europe, Canada and the US combined have grown from 2.9 GWh in 2020 to almost 79 GWh in 2025, representing a more than 25-fold increase.

title: Tongwei launches TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48 rooftop solar module with 24.5% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Unveiled at Solar & Storage Live UK, the new module combines high power output, strong energy yield, and broad adaptability in a compact format, delivering up to 490 W with an efficiency of 24.5%.
28 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
Tongwei Solar has launched TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48, a new 48-cell module adopting a mainstream format of 1762*1134*30 mm, designed for rooftop applications where available space, installation conditions, and aesthetic requirements can vary significantly.
Built on Tongwei’s TNC technology platform, the product delivers up to 490 W with an efficiency of 24.5%, helping rooftop systems achieve higher installed capacity while maintaining strong energy performance under varying operating conditions. TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48 provides a 30 W power gain per module compared to conventional TOPCon modules, enabling higher installed capacity on the same roof area and helping make better use of limited rooftop space.
Field testing showed an average 3.3% gain in per-watt generation compared with conventional BC modules under the tested conditions (Figure 1). During the low-light periods of early morning and late afternoon, the generation gain reached up to 12.32% (Figure 2). This capability is especially valuable when irradiance is low but electricity prices may be higher under time-of-use tariffs.
Figure 1: Daily per-watt generation comparison: TNC vs. conventional BC modules (Tongwei Yancheng Test Base)
Figure 2: TNC generation gain peaks during high-value, early morning, and late afternoon hours
In the tested scenario, TNC achieved 447.56 equivalent full-load hours, compared with 433.27 hours for conventional BC modules, representing approximately 3.3% higher generation capability. The time-of-use electricity calculation showed an additional revenue of around €0.03 per day under the tested conditions.
TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48 can also offer a competitive upfront cost by delivering more energy output with lower CAPEX, saving over €400 in initial module investment for a standard 12-module system compared to conventional BC modules.
Adaptability for real-world conditions
TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48 is built to maintain energy performance across a broad range of real-world conditions. In Germany-based simulations, TNC showed only 0.38% energy loss related to roof tilt under low-light conditions, compared with 0.96% for conventional BC modules. This means conventional BC modules were more than 2.5 times more sensitive to tilt in the tested scenario. At a fixed 40° tilt, TNC recorded approximately 1.02%–1.11% low-light generation loss across different orientations, compared with 3.53%–3.72% for conventional BC modules.
TNC technology also maintains a lower power-loss ratio under different soiling conditions. Compared with conventional BC modules, the reduction in fractional power loss reached 0.40 percentage points under light soiling, 0.73 percentage points under moderate soiling and 0.99 percentage points under heavy soiling.
Beyond performance adaptability, TNC 2.0 FULLX G12R-48 is offered in full black and black frame options, giving customers more freedom in system configuration, operating conditions, and rooftop aesthetics, while delivering more energy from limited roof space.

title: Austria to enable peer-to-peer electricity sharing from October - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Austria will introduce peer-to-peer electricity sharing from Oct. 5, initially allowing participation between metering points served by the same grid operator. Reduced grid charges for peer-to-peer arrangements are expected to take effect from January 2027, with nationwide implementation planned from April 2027.
Petra Hannen
28 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
New rules governing shared electricity use will come into force in Austria on Oct. 1.
Under the new framework, individuals and legal entities will be able to share self-generated electricity without establishing a separate legal entity.
Processing and billing can take place directly between the contracting parties or through a service provider or registered organizer. Unlike energy communities, peer-to-peer arrangements may be operated for profit.
The model will initially be subject to geographical restrictions. For the time being, only metering points assigned to the same grid operator will be able to participate. According to the coordination office, implementation across multiple grid areas, enabling nationwide electricity sharing, is expected from April 2027.
Reduced grid charges
A transition period will also apply to grid charges. An amended regulation governing grid charges is currently scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. From that date, planned reductions in grid charges will apply to local and regional citizen energy communities, peer-to-peer arrangements, and joint generation facilities.
As a result, while peer-to-peer electricity sharing can begin within the local and regional areas of a single grid operator from Oct. 5, grid operators will not be able to apply reduced grid charges between October and December 2026.
According to the coordination office, only members of local or regional renewable energy communities will remain eligible for reduced grid usage charges until the end of 2026.
Reduced grid tariffs are planned for peer-to-peer contracts between metering points located close to one another. To qualify, participants will have to define a specific “proximity zone” when registering. The framework distinguishes between main line, site, local and regional zones.

title: World's most powerul Starship rocket reaches orbit, deploys 26 Starlink satellites
content: The world’s largest and most powerful launch vehicle, SpaceX’s Starship, has just launched into orbit for the first time and deployed 26 of the company’s higher-performing Starlink V3 internet satellites. The uncrewed Starship Flight 14 lifted from the company’s Starbase site in Texas at around 7:46 am CT, on Monday, September 28. The historic departure marked the vehicle’s 14th integrated flight and the first aimed at sending the vehicle into orbit around Earth. The 407-foot-tall (124 meter) rocket consists of the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage. If the mission proceeds as planned, Starship will reportedly complete about six orbits around Earth during a nearly 10-hour flight, its longest mission to date. It will then splash down in the Pacific Ocean west of Chile. The flight also marks the first time Starship is carrying operational satellites into space. “Payload deploy complete. All 26 Starlink V3 satellites are in orbit,” one of SpaceX’s latest posts on the social media platform X, stated. First flight headed for orbitSpaceX plans to deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites during Flight 14, marking the first operational satellite deployment from Starship. Every satellite is designed to add one terabit per second (Tbps) of capacity to the company’s internet network.Together, the 26 satellites could add a total of 26 Tbps of capacity, which is about 10 times as much as a single Falcon 9 launch carrying V2 Mini Starlink satellites. In addition, the satellites are set to unfold their antennas and solar arrays. They will then make initial contact with ground stations as well as the rest of the Starlink constellation through radio-frequency and laser links.Starship completing its ascent burn. Credit: SpaceX / ScreenshotThey will afterward use their onboard thrusters to raise their orbits and undergo checks before beginning service. “Following their on-orbit checkouts the satellites should begin serving customers as soon as a few weeks after launch,” SpaceX representatives, said.What’s more, SpaceX has equipped three of the satellites with cameras made to look back at Starship and capture images of its heat shield following deployment. The images will allow the team to better study the condition of Starship’s thermal protection system, as SpaceX works toward eventually returning the spacecraft directly to its launch site.Six trips around EarthAll 13 previous Starship flights since 2023 were suborbital. Flight 14 is designed to send the spacecraft into orbit for the first time. Starship is expected to fly roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth.Nevertheless, the spacecraft will only perform its orbital insertion burn after flight controllers confirm there is sufficient redundancy in systems necessary for its later deorbit burn. By the end of the mission, it will fire a single Raptor engine in space to leave orbit before making a controlled reentry and splashdown.Starship deploying its payload of 26 Starlink V3 satellites.Credit: SpaceX / ScreenshotFlight 14 also includes changes after the previous test. During Starship’s Flight 13, Super Heavy used all 33 engines for its boostback burn for the first time. Ice later clogged three center engines, and ended the maneuver early. The firm therefore made hardware changes to improve engine filtering and software changes aimed at improving relight reliability.SpaceX is further testing several heat-shield upgrades on Starship. These include additional mechanisms to keep tiles attached and curved tiles designed to reduce heating in the gaps between them. Two heat-shield tiles recovered from Ship 40 are being used again on Ship 41. This is the first time Starship has reused heat-shield tiles.

title: New solar cells reach 30.1% efficiency with smarter perovskite layers
content: Researchers at Nanjing University in China and collaborating institutions have developed a novel processing strategy to resolve a major efficiency issue in monolithic all-perovskite triple-junction solar cells.In particular, a surface reconstruction and halide homogenization strategy has been designed to address performance-limiting issues in 2.0-eV ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) perovskite films.It led to the development of the perovskite triple-junction solar cell with an impressive 30.1 percent power conversion efficiency (certified at 29.3 percent). As per the study, this integrated design operates with high stability under continuous use and could push future multi-layered solar cell efficiencies beyond 35 percent.New fabrication strategyStandard silicon panels currently dominate the solar industry, but face physical limits that restrict how much sunlight they can convert into energy. Perovskites offer a promising alternative, as these synthetic materials can be stacked in layers to absorb a wider range of wavelengths across the solar spectrum more efficiently.To capture high-energy sunlight, scientists build ultrawide-bandgap (2.0-eV) perovskite films rich in bromide. But high bromide content behaves unpredictably during fabrication. The top surface dries and crystallizes first. The bottom remains wet.This mismatch creates a rigid outer skin over a fluid core, causing the film to wrinkle, crack, and segregate its chemical ingredients. As a result, the energy is wasted, and severe voltage losses occur.Researchers solved this issue by creating a dual processing technique that smooths the material surface and manages how the crystals form. It resolved the uneven drying issue by combining a targeted solvent bath with a small amount of oleylammonium chloride additive. The balanced solvent treatment reshapes and flattens the top layer, while the chloride addition forces the bromide and iodide components to crystallize at the same time. This joint approach prevents premature surface hardening, creating a smooth and structurally uniform film throughout the entire material.Shows promise in testing A monolithic triple-junction cell combines three interconnected light-absorbing layers, each designed with a distinct bandgap to target different parts of the solar spectrum.Elimination of surface wrinkles and structural defects led to the optimization of all three layers of the solar cell for peak energy capture. The top 2.0-eV subcell achieved a high open-circuit voltage of 1.46 V, paired with a 1.60-eV middle layer for spectrum matching and a 1.22-eV bottom layer for deep infrared absorption. Together, this monolithic triple-junction configuration delivered a record 30.1 percent power conversion efficiency, which was independently certified at 29.3 percent.“The resulting UWBG perovskite films show uniform surface potential, suppressed non-radiative recombination, improved carrier mobility and an open-circuit voltage of 1.46 V,” the researchers noted. It works, and it even lasts. Reportedly, the finished cell retained over 90% of its initial efficiency after 569 hours of continuous, maximum-power operation under simulated suns.After completing initial laboratory testing, the team aims to reduce voltage and fill-factor losses, refine current matching, and scale up device size for larger applications. Future studies will shift from initial efficiency measurements to evaluating module performance under realistic operating conditions, with a specific focus on radiation, ultraviolet, vacuum, and thermal-cycling durability for potential space missions.And because it avoids heavy silicon wafers, it points toward ultralight, flexible solar modules designed for commercial roofs, wearable electronics, and satellite deployments.

title: Boston Dynamics starts training for Atlas robots at Hyundai plant
content: The viral parkour stunts and backflips are officially over. Boston Dynamics is putting its famous humanoid robot, Atlas, to work on the factory floor. Boston Dynamics has launched the Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC) inside Hyundai Motor Group’s Metaplant America campus near Savannah, Georgia. The goal is to establish a dedicated testbed and training hub for physical AI and commercial robotics.Hyundai plans to deploy 25,000 Atlas units across its global Hyundai and Kia facilities over the coming years, culminating in full autonomous component assembly and heavy-load labor by 2030.“Together with Hyundai Motor Group, we are pioneering physical AI at enterprise scale,” said Zack Jackowski, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Boston Dynamics. “We have established a clear strategy to optimize our supply chain, production, testing, and deployment capabilities for Atlas. RMAC reinforces our shared ambition to create a future where robots amplify human potential by making work safer and more productive.” Large-scale deploymentIn the last few years, millions watched Atlas perform jaw-dropping acrobatics in lab videos. Now, human trainers teleoperate the robots in real-world factory conditions, teaching them to handle automotive parts logistics, sequence assembly lines, and organize heavy components. By 2030, plans call for Atlas to handle full component assembly and take on dangerous, back-breaking labor. Atlas can lift up to 50 kg (110 lbs) peak and maintain a 30 kg (66 lbs) continuous payload. It has a ~4-hour operating runtime and supports autonomous battery swaps for round-the-clock factory operations. Equipped with custom tactile grippers for handling automotive components, the robot boasts 56 total degrees of freedom. The autonomous robot is also built to handle harsh workplace environments, performing reliably in temperatures from freezing lows of -20°C to highs of 40°C (-4°F to 104°F).Hyundai is not experimenting on the margins. The auto giant plans to deploy 25,000 Atlas units across its global Hyundai and Kia manufacturing plants over the coming years. To supply that massive fleet, the Group will build a dedicated U.S. production facility capable of churning out 30,000 robots every single year.Boston Dynamics and Hyundai Motor Group are scaling up humanoid automation in phases, starting with Atlas robots currently handling real-world parts sorting, logistics, and sequencing at the RMAC facility. Operations will relocate to a dedicated facility ten times larger in 2027 to expand testing into non-automotive sectors. Easing human tasks Hyundai expects Atlas robots to enter component assembly lines within the decade, laying the framework for broader industrial adoption. The humanoid units will eventually handle heavy lifting, repetitive movements, and complex manufacturing operations across various production sites. This transition aims to reduce physical strain on human workers by shifting high-risk and strenuous tasks directly to automation.Growing workplace automation prompted Kia Corp’s labor union to request a dedicated body to safeguard labor rights in the AI era. Earlier, Hyundai Motor Vice Chair Jaehoon Chang addressed these anxieties about potential job losses and stated that workforce demands will persist because human personnel will remain essential to operate, train, and maintain the robotic fleet.Furthermore, Boston Dynamics is actively collaborating with existing clients to export Atlas beyond auto plants into aerospace, semiconductor fabrication, and life sciences.

title: China claims 16,172-foot drilling feat with ocean hard rock recovery
content: China’s Mengxiang (Dream) ocean drilling vessel has reached a new deep-sea drilling milestone after recovering basalt from the South China Sea basin, China’s Ministry of Natural Resources said Monday. The vessel completed a 30-day scientific drilling trial and returned to Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, after drilling to a maximum depth of 16,172 feet (4,929.17 meters).During the mission, Mengxiang achieved a maximum total water depth of 4,929.17 meters (16,172 feet) and drilled to a maximum penetration of 864.77 meters (2,837 feet). The results set a new national record for independently conducted deep-sea drilling in China.The mission focused on testing the vessel and its scientific drilling systems in ultra-deep water. It also allowed researchers to collect geological material from the ocean basin and evaluate equipment under demanding conditions.China has now joined the U.S. and Japan as the third country to retrieve hard-rock samples from a deep-sea ocean basin using a drilling vessel.Basalt core recovered from seafloorResearchers used self-developed rotary coring tools to recover a 4.27-meter-long (14-foot-long) basalt core. The sample provides direct material from the deep-ocean crust for geological studies.The expedition also established a coring system designed to meet standards set by the International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP). During several operations, core-recovery rates exceeded 100 percent. The team said its coring efficiency, sample quality, and operational stability reached advanced IODP benchmarks.The ability to recover long and intact rock sections is important for researchers studying the structure and history of the ocean floor. The cores can preserve physical and chemical evidence of geological processes that occurred over long periods.China's Mengxiang (Dream) ocean drilling vessel has set a national record in deep-sea drilling, elevating its capability to the 5,000-meter level, after obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Monday. pic.twitter.com/4oPIzhrKi0— People's Daily, China (@PDChina) September 28, 2026ROVs operate at 13,123 feetThe mission also tested underwater robotic systems during extended operations. For the first time, ship-borne remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) carried out long-duration, high-intensity coordinated work during the drilling mission.Two ROVs accumulated more than 358 working hours at depths of 4,000 meters (13,123 feet). One continuous operation lasted as long as 103 hours. The performance was described as reaching international advanced levels.The team also developed a risk-prevention and emergency-response system for ultra-deep-water drilling. Together, these capabilities demonstrate China’s ability to manage a complete scientific drilling workflow in extreme water depths.Core samples could reveal South China Sea historyFor the first time, the team processed and analyzed the recovered cores according to IODP procedures. The work covered collection, documentation, description, sectioning, scanning, sampling, testing and archiving.The cruise produced a large volume of rock cores and scientific data. Researchers expect the material to help address questions surrounding seafloor spreading and the geological development of the South China Sea.The samples could also provide evidence about how the basin formed and evolved. Beyond geological research, the results may support studies of the region’s paleo-environmental history and contribute to research related to energy exploration and development in ultra-deep waters.

title: 4th-gen light source takes China closer to building a super microscope
content: The Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF) in China has fired its first electron beam, which reached energy levels of 2.2 billion electron volts (eV), marking a major step toward China’s ambitious goal of building a fourth-generation light source. This opens up a myriad of research avenues from chip manufacturing to Alzheimer’s disease. A synchrotron light source is electromagnetic radiation produced using particle accelerators or storage rings. Once a high-energy beam of light is produced, it can be bent using magnets and used to probe matter or living cells at sub-nanometer scales, making them quite effective as super microscopes. Although generating light in this way is expensive, it is a highly reliable way to generate wideband radiation in the far-infrared wavelength range. These devices were first built for high-energy particle physics but later modified to serve as light sources. It was only in the third generation of these devices that low emittance was prioritized to generate highly focused and small beams of light. Fourth generation light sourceChina built its first light source at Hefei in 1989 and deployed it for research for finding the structure of the Sars virus, for imaging a dinosaur inside 99-million-year-old amber and how arsenic could treat leukemia. The Asian giant also boasts of the High Energy Photon Source in Beijing and Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility and began construction of the Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF) in Anhui province in 2023. The project is expected to be completed by 2028 and together with the other two light sources, will help China cover high, medium and low-energy ranges for advanced light systems. HALF is a fourth-generation light source and is designed to use extremely bright X-rays. These rays are generated by turning high-speed electrons in magnetic fields. Fourth-generation light sources are better than third-generation sources such as the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory or the Advanced Light Source at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since they produce finer beams that are more concentrated and generate brighter X-rays. Light at HALFHALF uses a 630-foot (192 m) long linear accelerator to accelerate electrons. In their recent run, the team achieved an energy of 2.2 billion eV, marking a major milestone for the project. X-rays produced at HALF are expected to be 100 times brighter and also more coherent than its predecessor and are claimed to be the brightest and most stable in the world. The facility also features 35 experimental stations that will be deployed for research in high-temperature superconductivity, new energy batteries, materials as well as life sciences research. The first batch of these stations will also feature a platform for extreme ultraviolet lithography, a technology key for making advanced semiconductors. This is currently part of the US’ strict export controls and will open doors for China to work with this technology. “Producing a beam successfully means we’ve taken a key step towards our final goal,” said He Zhigang, a scientist working on the project, told state news agency Xinhua.

title: F-22 Raptor spotted testing new sensors during aggressive maneuvers
content: The U.S. Air Force appears to be expanding flight testing of passive-sensing equipment for the F-22A Raptor after a fighter carrying low-observable underwing pods was photographed during aggressive maneuvers near Edwards Air Force Base on September 25, 2026. Mojave Planespotting images show the Raptor flying with the pods seen days earlier.The activity suggests testing has moved beyond basic carriage. The Air Force could be examining whether infrared or electro-optical sensors remain effective during demanding maneuvers. Such systems could help the F-22 detect and track threats without continuously using radar.F-22 expands its flight-test envelopeThe September 25 imagery followed photographs released on September 19 showing an F-22 using the callsign FEVER21 over California’s Aerospace Valley. The aircraft carried two angular pods beneath its outer wings. One appeared to feature a transparent aperture consistent with an infrared or electro-optical sensor.The Air Force has not disclosed their functions.Aggressive maneuvering exposes external equipment to aerodynamic loads, vibration, and changing airflow. Testing could examine sensor stability and performance as the aircraft rapidly changes attitude.F-22 with stealth IRST pods does aggressive maneuvers over Edwards AFB. pic.twitter.com/UzhYXHw4WV— Mojave Planespotting (@MojaveSpotter) September 25, 2026Passive detection adds new optionsAn infrared search-and-track capability could give the F-22 another method for detecting airborne targets while limiting radar emissions. Infrared sensors detect thermal signatures and provide information based on a different physical phenomenon from radar.That could be valuable against aircraft designed to reduce their radar signatures. IRST systems can be affected by atmospheric conditions and background clutter.Combining infrared information with radar, electronic-support systems and offboard targeting data could give pilots a battlespace picture. It also fits the Air Force’s push toward networked, emission-controlled air combat.Sensor program reaches key stageThe testing aligns with the F-22 Sensor Enhancements program. The Government Accountability Office said an earlier effort conducted six sensor-enhancement flight demonstrations in 2024 before the follow-on program was established.In July 2026, GAO reported that the first F-22 flight test using sensor-enhancement hardware had slipped from March to May after a subcomponent failure delayed deliveries. The setback reduced testing time before the planned September 2026 completion of the program’s Middle Tier of Acquisition phase.The Air Force also procured hardware in advance for 30 sensor-enhancement sets.Raptor modernization meets F-47 eraEarlier 2026 imagery showed an F-22 carrying stealth-shaped external fuel tanks and faceted mission pods, suggesting work on range and passive sensing.The latest testing comes as the Air Force develops the F-47 under its Next Generation Air Dominance program. Boeing was selected for the F-47 Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract in 2025.There is no public evidence that the F-22 pods directly test F-47 hardware. The Raptor can provide a platform for developing passive detection and sensor fusion techniques.The sightings do not establish what the pods contain, but the September 25 maneuvering indicates increasingly demanding flight testing.

title: World-first: Quantum computer operated in space despite setbacks
content: Scientists at the University of Vienna have achieved a global first after operating a quantum computer in space. The computer was launched on a Falcon 9 rocket in June 2025. It could only be operated after much tribulation, showcasing the challenges of operating new technologies in the harsh environments of space. The idea to launch a quantum computer to space was also a response to another challenge being faced in space- the data bottleneck for satellites. While companies like SpaceX have made it easier to launch missions into orbit, the challenges of operating them are much the same. Satellites are great at collecting raw data but do not carry compute that can process it. This means that all captured data must first be sent back to Earth to make sense of it. However, this creates a bottleneck because downlink bandwidth and ground-station availability limit how much data is received. A possible alternative to this is to process the data on the satellite itself, and a quantum solution would be ideal. Quantum computer in spaceIt is common knowledge now that qubits, or quantum bits that store information in quantum computers, are extremely sensitive to outside disturbances. The orbital environment that satellites operate in does not offer the highly controlled environments of quantum laboratories, which can shield the system. Before a quantum computer can operate, it must be launched on a rocket, and its components undergo severe mechanical stress before reaching orbit. Researchers from the University of Vienna reinforced the computer components using titanium baseplates and fragile optical fibers using epoxy, Even after extensive vibration testing before launch, only three of the six silicon single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) on the computer, needed to detect photons, survived the trip. The harsh sunlight of space created huge background noise for the SPADs to make any measurements. So, scientists used the brief 30-minute periods that the satellite passes in the Earth’s shadow to make the measurements. Radiation and Laser problemsIn case you were of the view that hurdles were now behind them and the team could focus on data processing, that would still have a been a smooth ride to get to this point. Once the sunlight issue was resolved, the researchers faced radiation hurdles from the Van Allen belts created by the Earth’s magnetic field and which traps photons and electrons. The team anticipated this when preparing for put the quantum computer in space and encased the device in centimeter-thick, aerospace-grade aluminum. The casing worked for the electrons but couldn’t keep protons at bay, which degraded the photon detectors.The adhesive used to keep the laser in place also degraded in vacuum and contaminated its optics, which reduced the laser’s output from 20 milliwatts to four milliwatts. Even after much tribulation, the researchers were finally able to test if photons traveling through the instrument’s circuits were indistinguishable. Based on experiments on Earth, this was expected to happen when temperatures of the crystals producing the photons reached 90.5 degrees Fahrenheit (32.5 degrees Celsius), and that’s exactly what the team saw in space. While this doesn’t help process satellite data in space yet, it shows that quantum processors can be compressed, can operate in space, and can be used to establish quantum links between satellites and the ground. The research findings are on the preprint server arXiv.

title: UK base with US bombers targeted in suspected bomb plot, police says
content: Five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in southwest England on September 27 after police received a report about three suspicious vans heading toward the air base. The arrests came as the British base was hosting U.S. B-1B Lancer bombers that have been used in operations against Iran.Armed British police stopped the men near the Gloucestershire airfield and detained them on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Explosive ordnance disposal teams were sent to inspect the vehicles, while authorities evacuated 85 homes in nearby Whelford as a precaution.U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been seeking to cause “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and U.S. authorities.Police respond to suspicious vehiclesCounter Terrorism Policing said officers received a call at about 12:45 a.m. local time reporting three vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford.Five men were subsequently arrested by armed officers and remained in custody as investigators worked to establish what happened. Police said the incident was contained and placed a 400-meter (1,312-foot) cordon around the area.“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said.“As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”British Army bomb disposal teams examined the three vans. Video aired by British news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting white vans near the base perimeter.Security tightened around RAF FairfordThe incident prompted a major security response around the airfield. Armed officers patrolled the area while roadblocks and heavy equipment were positioned near the base.“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.Gloucestershire Police said the cordon was a precaution and warned residents that emergency services would remain in the area for some time.“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution, and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”The base had already been operating under increased security for several days, according to people familiar with the matter.Base hosts US B-1B bombersRAF Fairford does not have permanently assigned U.S. Air Force aircraft. However, it supports American operations and has long served as a major U.S. bomber location in Europe.About a dozen B-1Bs have been stationed there for around seven months. The aircraft were heavily involved in Operation Epic Fury, when the base hosted about two dozen B-1Bs and B-52 Stratofortresses during the U.S. air campaign against Iran.Trump described the arrests as “fantastic” before departing on Air Force One on September 27.“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump said. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”The U.S. Air Force said it was working with British authorities to protect personnel and installations.UK investigates suspected bomb plotThe U.K. government authorized U.S. strikes from RAF Fairford against Iranian missile sites earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps later warned that it considered the base a legitimate target, according to reports.“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said.“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”Another British base hosting U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, where F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters are stationed. British and U.S. authorities said investigations into the Fairford incident remain ongoing.

title: Hyperbolic wave attractors could power next-generation optical chips
content: Scientists found a way to stop light and sound waves from scattering chaotically inside complex, oddly shaped spaces.Shout into an irregularly shaped room, and your voice shatters into a chaotic mess of echoes. The incoming wave hits a slanted wall, bounces off at an angle, and rapidly spirals into complete unpredictability. Physicists call this non-linear mess a “dynamical billiard.” It is the bane of optical engineers and acoustic designers. Now, scientists have found a way to stop the madness.Researchers at the Advanced Science Research Center at the CUNY Graduate Center (CUNY ASRC) have discovered that passing waves through a special class of synthetic media forces them to abandon chaotic scattering entirely. Instead of splintering, the waves naturally organize themselves into repeating geometric loops.The discovery could reshape how engineers route light on computer chips, direct wireless signals, and build biological sensors.“This work shows how geometry and the properties of a material can work together to produce wave behavior that is both surprising and useful,” said Andrea Alù, the study’s principal investigator. “By understanding how waves organize themselves in these hyperbolic media, we can begin to explore new approaches to controlling energy, information, and communication signals in complex environments,” Alù added. The geometry of orderThe research team aimed to investigate how combining these non-standard reflection properties with an asymmetrical cavity reshapes wave dynamics.In everyday materials, reflection obeys a simple rule: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Throw light into an oddly shaped box, and those reflections quickly turn messy.Standard materials send reflecting waves outward at equal angles, creating unpredictable chaotic patterns inside irregular containers. Hyperbolic materials overcome this limitation by restricting wave propagation along narrow, highly directed paths and altering reflection behavior off slanted surfaces. Inside these specialized cavities, waves progressively organize into stable, scale-invariant closed loops as broken mirror symmetry and shrinking wavelengths collapse chaotic scattering into structured trajectories.This unique propagation gives rise to wave trajectories with directional rotation, or handedness, which dictates whether paths rotate clockwise or counterclockwise. Researchers experimentally validated this self-organizing behavior by controlling vibrations within an engineered mechanical metamaterial.“The most exciting aspect of these results is that they connect a simple geometric idea with a rich set of wave phenomena,” said Enrico Renzi, a doctoral student in Alù’s lab. “We can observe how the waves become organized, and we can connect that organization to properties such as stability and handedness. This gives us a framework for designing wave behavior rather than simply observing it.”Ocean rootsThe physics behind this tabletop development shares surprising roots with deep-sea oceanography.In the ocean, underwater waves travel through layers of water with differing densities. When these internal waves hit underwater slopes, they reflect in unusual ways, often locking into closed trajectories that concentrate energy beneath the surface.The CUNY team translated this fluid-dynamics concept into a solid-state platform using a mechanical metamaterial — a custom-designed structure with miniature pillars that guide elastic vibrations.The usage could go beyond mechanical vibrations. The same mathematical framework applies to 2D materials like hexagonal boron nitride and molybdenum trioxide, which host hybrid light-matter excitations called hyperbolic phonon polaritons.Researchers aim to harness wave attractors to construct low-loss nanophotonic circuits, engineer highly sensitive biosensors, manipulate microscopic particles using light, and create wave-based analog computing systems.The study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

title: Cocaine plays with mind, hijacks brain circuit, drives repetitive behavior
content:
The team captured behavior as an observer
The team confirmed that disruption of the capacity to define actions is associated with the development of repetitive and rigid/maladaptive behaviors seen in a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including Tourette syndrome, Parkinson’s disease and drug-induced movement disorders.
“We wanted to capture behavior as an observer actually sees it: grooming, licking, exploring, but  this was impossible to score manually,” said Itay Shalom, a PhD student from Hebrew University of Jerusalem. “STEREO allowed us to track the entire behavioral repertoire progressively narrowed until one type of action came to dominate.”
Repeated exposure to cocaine
Using repeated exposure to cocaine as an experimental model of behavioral rigidity, the researchers observed a striking shift. Diverse and exploratory behavior gradually gave way to persistent repetition. By the fifth day of exposure, licking the floor and walls of the enclosure accounted for more than 60% of the observed time. These behaviors were rarely seen in the absence of cocaine, illustrating how a normally varied set of actions can become restricted to a persistent behavioral pattern, according to a press release.
The team also mapped this change to the ventrolateral striatum (VLS), an area of the striatum involved particularly in movements of the mouth and tongue. Within this region are two major neural pathways, known as the direct and indirect pathways, which appear to exert opposing influences over which actions are expressed.
When the researchers activated neurons belonging to the indirect pathway, the cocaine-driven repetitive behavior was immediately interrupted, and behavior shifted toward alternative actions. Once the stimulation was terminated, the effect rapidly reversed and repetitive behavior resumed. Suppressing this same pathway produced the opposite result, limiting the ability to switch behavior, driving longer bouts of the repetitive behavior, as per the release.
The research team revealed that the direct pathway showed the opposite pattern. Reducing its activity weakened the drug-induced repetitive behavior, while activating it in the absence of cocaine was itself sufficient to produce rigid patterns of repetitive actions resembling those observed following drug exposure.
“Cocaine does not appear to create an entirely new behavioral program,” said Ben Jerry Gonzales, a student of Hebrew University. “It takes control of a circuit the brain already uses for natural actions and pushes behavior toward persistent repetition.”
The team also pointed out that the same circuit is responsible for the expression of normal, context-appropriate grooming and licking. Cocaine therefore appears to hijack a normal action-selection system rather than recruit a circuit dedicated to abnormal behavior.
The findings may help researchers better understand how repetitive motor behaviors emerge across different neurological and psychiatric conditions. Because different areas of the striatum correspond to different types of movement, the researchers propose that similar imbalances in other striatal circuits could potentially contribute to other forms of behavioral rigidity, as per the release.

title: OpenAI agents hit UN website more than 16,000 times, bypassed a filter
content: OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents repeatedly queried a UN website and used techniques that appeared to circumvent restrictions when trying to retrieve publicly available data, according to an independent research report based on information supplied by AI research firm Transluce. The agents scanned a public data hub operated by UN Trade and Development, the UN’s trade arm, more than 16,000 times between April and the end of June, highlighting a growing problem with AI agents that can independently navigate the web and take actions when they encounter obstacles.Researchers believe the models were initially tasked with finding publicly available information, but their behavior became increasingly aggressive when the website prevented them from accessing some of the requested data.Pushing past website restrictionsAccording to researcher and report author Rowan Howard-Jones, the agents encountered a filter that blocked their requests and subsequently found a way around it, with the technique they ultimately used not permitted by the website operators.Additionally, the agents were apparently not instructed to attack or compromise the UN website. Instead, the behavior emerged while they were attempting to complete an information-retrieval task, the Wall Street Journal reports.Cybersecurity expert Alex Stamos, a lecturer at Stanford University, told WSJ that the UN incident as “borderline” hacking, while describing it primarily as extremely aggressive scraping and data retrieval.The UN activity is one of several recent cases in which OpenAI’s models have behaved unexpectedly while operating on the internet. OpenAI said it is conducting a broad review of “misaligned models during training and evaluation” and examining a large volume of actions taken by its agents. The company said most of the activity it has reviewed involved routine research tasks, including retrieving publicly available web content, but acknowledged that organizations affected by the behavior have legitimate concerns. OpenAI added that it has notified dozens of organizations about cases in which its models bypassed security controls or negatively affected websites.The problem with giving AI agents more autonomyRecent incidents have included activity involving US government websites, including the Commerce Department and Securities and Exchange Commission, while Australian officials have launched an inquiry after saying an OpenAI agent hacked one of their government websites.Other researchers have reported agents creating fake email addresses, bypassing website rate limits and falsely claiming they were not bots. The UN incident therefore adds another example to a growing body of evidence that autonomous AI systems can interpret obstacles as problems to be solved rather than boundaries that must be respected. Researchers also argue that the underlying issue is not necessarily that the models are deliberately trying to cause damage, but the notion that agents are increasingly capable of pursuing a goal through multiple steps without waiting for a human to approve each action.“Agents gradually refined their methods to retrieve more data from each scan, eventually discovering that a game by Google could be used to fetch data in bulk,” Howard-Jones wrote in the report.Furthermore, the latest incidents are likely to intensify debate over how much autonomy AI agents should have when interacting with external systems, raising additional questions about whether existing website security mechanisms are sufficient when facing software that can reason about those mechanisms and modify its behavior.

title: Boeing 737 MAX software glitch threatens jet delays, FAA orders checks
content: Boeing’s push to bring the final two 737 MAX variants into commercial service faces another potential setback after a software issue was found that can increase pilot workload during a specific missed-approach scenario.The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is now reviewing the problem and plans to convene a Corrective Action Review Board to determine whether it represents a flight-safety concern. The review comes just as Boeing appeared to be approaching certification of the 737 MAX 10 while preparing to begin deliveries of the recently certified MAX 7.The issue affects versions 14 and 14.1 of the software used by the 737 MAX flight management computer. Major US airlines including Alaska, American, Southwest and United have said their aircraft currently in service do not use the affected versions. Southwest and United have also told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft equipped with the software, instead opting for an earlier version.Software problem emerges during a missed approachThe problem involves the aircraft’s vertical navigation system (VNAV), which helps automatically manage altitude along a programmed flight path. Under a specific sequence of events, the issue can occur when pilots perform a go-around from a precision approach with the autopilot engaged and then modify the flight path programmed into the flight management computer. VNAV can disengage, leaving the aircraft with a lower level of automated pitch control.The autopilot remains available, and Boeing says pilots are trained to fly the aircraft safely without VNAV. However, the loss of the automated function can increase the crew’s workload at a particularly demanding point in a flight, when the aircraft is close to the ground, and the crew is already managing a missed landing.Boeing informed 737 operators about the problem last month and issued guidance reinforcing existing procedures for handling the situation. The company is also working on a permanent software fix, the Wall Street Journal reported.The issue was first reported to Boeing by an airline in November 2024. The company initially concluded in February 2025 that it did not constitute a safety issue, but additional information from operators later prompted Boeing to conduct a formal safety review.MAX 7 and MAX 10 caught in the reviewThe affected software is connected to both of Boeing’s newest MAX variants. The FAA certified the 737 MAX 7 in August with software version 14 installed. Southwest is expected to be its main early customer, but the airline has said it will not accept aircraft equipped with the affected software version.The larger MAX 10 used version 14.1 during certification testing. Boeing claimed that the aircraft had completed its flight-test program and was in the final documentation stage of the certification process.The MAX 10 is the largest member of the 737 family and is important to Boeing’s effort to address a large backlog of narrowbody orders. Any additional certification work could therefore create further complications for the program, which has already experienced years of delays.The FAA has further added that it will assess the software issue and take immediate action if the review identifies a safety concern. Boeing initially expected the permanent software correction to be ready in 2028, although the company is now working to accelerate the timetable.

title: US and China seek new military pact after Trump-Xi summit
content: China and the United States have agreed to pursue a new military crisis-communication agreement after President Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit to Washington from September 23 to 25.Military officials closely watched the discussions leading up to and during the summit between Washington and Beijing, South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported.One official described the public dialogue between Washington and Beijing as a “confidence builder for everybody.” Another U.S. military official said that “the US’ goal is to enable both strategic stability and deterrence by denial, and I believe respectful and professional communication with China does not preclude that.”During Xi’s three-day visit, he and President Donald Trump discussed strategic stability and major international and regional issues. China’s Foreign Ministry said the talks produced eight other “deliverables and understandings,” including trade, artificial intelligence, and counternarcotics cooperation.The Chinese and U.S. militaries agreed to conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention “as soon as possible,” and to continue the search for missing service members in China, according to a September 26 readout from China’s Foreign Ministry.Details of the military mechanism remain unclearThe two sides were preparing measures to activate additional military communication channels and strengthen existing ones, SCMP reported ahead of the summit.But the two militaries already have consultation arrangements and senior communication channels. Beijing’s announcement did not explain whether the proposed memorandum would establish a new hotline, create procedures for using existing connections, or define which incidents would trigger crisis consultations.Nevertheless, during his visit, Xi noted that military communication between the two countries needed improvement.“Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention,” Xi said at the Arrival Ceremony, as published by China’s Foreign Ministry.Xi linked military communication to his broader call to avoid confrontation between the two countries.“…we can certainly find the right path for our two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.US and Chinese commanders resume contactThe proposed memorandum follows renewed contact between senior U.S. and Chinese military commanders.Admiral Samuel Paparo, the senior U.S. commander in the Indo-Pacific, met General Yang Zhibin, commander of the People’s Liberation Army’s Eastern Theatre Command, during a defense conference in Victoria, British Columbia, in late August, according to the South China Morning Post.The SCMP reported that this first meeting ended a two-year interruption in theater-level contact between the two countries.Paparo and Yang discussed maintaining communication among senior leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and encourage safe and professional conduct by their forces.The military agreement was announced separately from the eight other summit deliverables listed by China’s Foreign Ministry. Among them, the two countries agreed to establish the China-U.S. AI Dialogue to exchange views on AI risks and benefits, with another exchange scheduled for November 2026.“China and the U.S. also agree to establish a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents,” the Foreign Ministry statement said in a September 26 release.On the military relationship, Beijing’s next step is to conclude the memorandum. But China has not provided a specific deadline, saying the two militaries had agreed to conclude the agreement “as soon as possible.”

title: New 20 MW Bronx battery site will deliver peak power to 20,000 homes
content: A new NineDot battery energy storage system in Hunts Point, the Bronx, will deliver nearly 20 megawatts to about 20,000 homes during peak grid hours.The company recently held a ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside elected officials, policymakers, and community organizations. Vanessa Gibson, Bronx Borough President, noted that the new storage system aims to address the environmental injustice and disinvestment the Bronx has long suffered.“We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said Adam Cohen, NineDot’s chief technology officer and co-founder. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.”The system is expected to be fully operational in time for next summer’s heat waves and will have enough capacity to power nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours.Battery storage targets peak demandAccording to NineDot, Hunts Point has faced significant pollution pressures for decades. More than 10,000 diesel trucks travel through the area each day, while two high-emissions peaker power plants operate in nearby Port Morris.In 2023, Hunts Point–Mott Haven recorded asthma-related emergency room visits at two to three times the citywide average, according to data cited in the release. Because the problem stems from fine particulate air pollution, energy storage will help retire gas-fired plants. As the NineDot battery storage site replaced the former home of a fuel oil trucking company, the project comes as New York City aims to transition to a cleaner, more resilient future by reducing its dependence on fossil-fuel “peaker” plants, which operate during periods of high electricity demand.NineDot said battery storage could also provide grid resiliency as Hunts Point moves toward electrification of its produce and fish market and truck fleet.“Battery energy storage is an important tool for modernizing New York’s electric grid and making it more resilient to extreme weather and high-stress conditions,” said David Sandbank, senior vice president at the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. “This Hunts Point project demonstrates how the right policies, partners and programs can deliver benefits for communities throughout New York City and beyond.”NineDot expands NYC battery fleetNineDot’s existing battery systems have already been deployed during periods of extreme electricity demand.During New York’s July 1-4, 2026 heat wave, nine NineDot battery projects exported nearly 34 megawatts during peak hours, as per the news release. The support was given to Con Edison’s local power network and the statewide power transmission system.That equates to removing the electricity demand of roughly 50,000 window air conditioners from the grid or powering approximately 34,000 households for four hours each day during peak demand.Currently, NineDot operates 11 projects across six locations in Staten Island and the Bronx, totaling 39 MW. The company also has more than 60 projects in development and a pipeline exceeding 1 GW.NineDot said it remains on track toward its goal of having 400 MW of battery storage in operation, under construction, or in development by the end of 2026.

title: These 5 companies are building America's rare earth supply chain
content: Rare earth elements are essential to electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics, semiconductors, and military systems. But building a reliable US supply chain requires more than finding deposits. Mining, refining, separating rare earths, and turning them into usable metals and magnets are all technically demanding processes.Five companies—Tactical Resources, USA Rare Earth, MP Materials, Energy Fuels, and NioCorp Developments—are pursuing different parts of that supply chain, from mining and processing to magnet manufacturing. Their projects range from operating facilities to early-stage developments.1. Tactical Resources is targeting heavy rare earths in TexasTactical Resources Corp. is advancing its Peak Project in Hudspeth County, Texas, approximately 90 miles southeast of El Paso. The project focuses on rare earth-enriched material already stockpiled at the Sierra Blanca Quarry after two decades of railway ballast production.The company says its analytical data show heavy rare earth elements and yttrium averaging more than twice the concentration of light rare earth elements. These materials are particularly relevant to the US supply chain because Western production and processing capacity is limited.In September 2026, Tactical outlined plans to advance metallurgical testing, permitting roadmaps, engineering work, and downstream partnerships. Initial testing by Kemetco Research reported total rare earth and yttrium extraction rates of up to 96.1 percent under heated hydrochloric acid conditions.However, these are preliminary, scoping-scale results, not demonstrated commercial recovery rates. The project has no established mineral resource or reserve estimate, and Tactical has not yet completed a preliminary economic assessment.2. USA Rare Earth is building an integrated supply chainUSA Rare Earth Inc. is pursuing a mine-to-magnet strategy that combines upstream mining and processing with rare earth metal and permanent magnet manufacturing.Its Round Top deposit in West Texas contains heavy rare earths and other critical minerals. The company also completed its combination with Brazil’s Serra Verde Group in September 2026, adding an operating mining and processing business in Goiás, Brazil.Serra Verde began production in January 2024. USA Rare Earth expects its first-stage operation to reach approximately 4,000 metric tons per year of total rare earth oxide production by the end of 2026.The company has also broken ground on a planned $1.2 billion rare earth metal and magnet manufacturing facility in Blacksburg, South Carolina. The facility is intended to expand US capacity to manufacture permanent magnets used in vehicles, electronics, and defense systems.3. MP Materials operates America’s Mountain Pass rare earth mineMP Materials Corp. operates the Mountain Pass rare earth mine and processing facility in California, one of the country’s established sources of domestically mined rare earth materials.The company is also expanding downstream operations, including metal, alloy, and magnet manufacturing at its Fort Worth, Texas, facility.In its second-quarter 2026 results, MP Materials reported neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) production of 840 metric tons, a 41 percent increase year over year. NdPr sales reached 1,006 metric tons, up 127 percent, while consolidated revenue rose 89 percent to $108.5 million.The company also signed a long-term agreement to supply separated gadolinium to an American aerospace and defense customer, expanding its heavy rare earth product portfolio.4. Energy Fuels is expanding rare earth processing in UtahEnergy Fuels Inc. is developing rare earth processing capacity at its White Mesa Mill in Utah, a facility traditionally associated with uranium processing.The company has begun construction on an approximately $104 million expansion intended to enable large-scale production of heavy rare earth oxides. The project is also expected to include a circuit for processing mixed rare earth carbonates from global feedstock sources.Energy Fuels has identified its planned Donald Project joint venture in Australia as a potential source of rare earth feedstock. It is also pursuing acquisitions intended to add rare earth metal, alloy, and magnet manufacturing capabilities.The White Mesa expansion is aimed at a key supply chain gap: converting rare earth-bearing materials into separated oxides that can be used in downstream manufacturing.5. NioCorp Developments is advancing a Nebraska critical minerals projectNioCorp Developments Ltd. is developing the Elk Creek Critical Minerals Project in southeast Nebraska. The planned operation is designed to produce several critical mineral products, including ferroniobium, scandium, titanium, and rare earth oxides.Its updated 2026 feasibility study outlines a proposed 40-year operation with a planned product slate that includes neodymium-praseodymium oxide, dysprosium oxide, and terbium oxide.The company has also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with Lockheed Martin to potentially purchase up to 15 metric tons of scandium oxide annually.Construction of the project’s main underground access portal began in February 2026. However, Elk Creek remains a development project, and its planned production should not be confused with output from an operating rare earth mine.Building a domestic rare earth supply chainThese five companies represent different approaches to expanding US access to rare earths. MP Materials already operates a domestic mine, while Energy Fuels is expanding processing capacity. USA Rare Earth is combining overseas production with US manufacturing, and Tactical Resources and NioCorp are advancing projects that have yet to reach commercial production.Securing rare earth supply requires more than mining the ore. Processing, separation, and manufacturing capacity will also determine how much of the supply chain can be established outside China. The company developments and project details in this article are based on information reported by American News Group in its September 22, 2026, PR Newswire release.
